subject: bat
reasoning:
I'm planning out a stylized bat model with realistic proportions—around a 0.5m wingspan and 0.12m body—while giving it exaggerated features like large ears, scalloped membrane wings, fangs, and glowing eyes, keeping the API calls simple and well-supported so the module runs correctly.

Now I'm sketching the skeleton: a rest pose with the bat standing on small feet with legs bent at hip, knee, and ankle, and wings spread sideways using membrane chains between the arm and finger bones, making sure the feet touch the ground plane properly.

I'll build the spine as a curved chain from hips to chest to neck to head, then sweep a tapered body shape along it with a dark purple-brown color. The head will be a separate rounded part attached to the head joint, and I'm now working out triangular extruded ears to attach on top.

Still working out ear placement...

Now I'm planning the wing structure — shoulder, elbow, and wrist joints forming each arm chain, with finger chains extending outward to support a membrane stretching between the fingertips and the body.

Thinking through membrane attachment points instead—maybe connecting the arm chain to flank-side points near the hips rather than trying to match finger chains directly, since both edges get resampled by arc length anyway. Sketching out the armL chain structure with shoulder, elbow, and wrist joints.

I realize the arm-to-finger membrane edges mismatch since the arm starts at the shoulder but the finger starts at the wrist, creating a fan-like shape rather than a clean panel. I need to reconsider the membrane boundary, perhaps running a flank path from the hip toward the shoulder to properly anchor the panel edge.

Instead, I decide to simplify by fanning membranes between consecutive finger chains (all rooted at the wrist) and closing with a final membrane running from the last finger down to a body-flank polyline connecting wrist-side to hip points. I'm placing wrist and fingertip coordinates to define the spread of digits, skipping the thumb as a separate claw and treating it as the leading arm edge, then working out where the trailing finger membrane should connect to the hip/ankle area to complete the wing shape.

I'll simplify by orienting all membrane edges consistently from the wrist side, using a body edge running shoulder-to-ankle to pair with the F3 finger chain. The resulting quad strip will be a bit twisted geometrically but should still read fine as a stylized bat wing membrane, so I'll accept that tradeoff rather than over-engineer the connection.

I'll accept some imperfection here and just build a stylized membrane wing with four panels connecting the finger chains to the flank, assigning thickness, color, and scallop values, with the flank edge bound to the hip joint for proper bone attachment.

For coloring I'm setting up mottled paint textures for the wing membrane and a countershading pattern for the body skin. For the face details I'm planning small sphere eyes, cone fangs, an extruded nose leaf, and claw spikes at the feet, with the head and muzzle built from spheres positioned relative to the head joint.

Still defining ear shapes...

For the torso I'm laying out a spine chain as a catmull-rom path from the hips up through the body, figuring out how many spine segments and names are needed to match the path's spans.

The head joint needs to attach to the final spine segment, so I'm adding a fourth name to account for the tip joint beyond the last span.

For the jaw, I want a small hinge parented under the head, positioned slightly forward and down for a bat-like snout, aiming toward where the mouth would open -- I'll include it since it was requested, even if minimal. Then I'm moving on to leg setup, rooted at the hips joint position.

Now I'm defining the leg chain with hip, knee, and foot joints, placing them sideways in typical bat hind-leg fashion, and tuning the ankle/foot position and radius so the foot capsule just touches the ground plane. I'm adding a small forward rod for the foot to suggest toes rather than building a full claw structure, then sweeping the leg with a tapering radius from hip to foot before moving on to sweep the wing arm chain next.

Still writing sweeps and details... I'm adding the fingers sweep, tweaking the wing membrane height, placing eye spheres in head-local coordinates, adding fang spikes at the jaw using direction/length/radius parameters, a small nose box, and starting the body spine sweep with a countershading taper.

Now I'm shaping the torso radius profile to be wider at the chest and narrower at the hips and neck, adding a head sphere offset slightly above the neck joint, placing ears, and settling on mottled and countershaded paint colors for the body and wing membrane, with the wing's flank edge anchored to the hips bone.

I'm figuring out joint references for the membrane edge, confirming the root sits near the ground with wingtips rising higher, and setting up the module's exported metadata and builder name. I'm being careful to only import the specific helper functions I actually use from the single library module, like catmull and paint functions, skipping randomness since none is needed. I'm also working out the naming convention for leg and wing-arm joint chains—since three points create two spans, I need three names total ending in the tip joint, like hip, knee, and ankle for each leg and shoulder, elbow, wrist for the wing arm.

Writing finger chain code...

Skipping the tail membrane for now and keeping a simple tail sweep instead. I'm setting up the fur, wing, ear, and eye color palette using countershade and mottle helpers, then starting the main builder function export.

Writing the spine chain and head joint...

Defining ear outline points...

I'm placing the ear using an extrude with position, thickness, and bevel settings relative to the head bone, keeping smoothing at 0 for sharper corners. Now I'm positioning the eye spheres using local coordinates offset from the head, checking the distance stays within the head sphere's radius.

I'm setting up the jaw joint with a parent-child relationship to the head bone, along with its aim direction, and then defining the jaw box geometry and fang spikes using local coordinates with base points, direction vectors, length, and radius.

Now I'm building the wing structure per side using chains: a shoulder-elbow-wrist arm chain parented to the spine's second joint, followed by digit chains for each finger attached from the wrist point to tip points, using named bones with "wing" and "digit" roles.

Then I'm defining membrane spans connecting each digit chain and the trailing flank chain to form the webbing between them, using scallop and thickness parameters for the wing surface, and linking the hind leg flank membrane back to the hip spine joint.

For the legs, I'm building a chain per side running from hip through knee to ankle, each with named joints and a "leg" role, checking the sweep radius so the foot doesn't sink too far below the ground plane. I'm then adding a toe rod extending from the leg tip, adjusting its endpoint height and radius so the foot's vertical sink stays within the allowed 2% tolerance relative to overall model height.

Now I'm sweeping the legs and wings with tapering radii for a furry look, and sweeping the finger chains at a fixed small radius. I'm also building a short tail chain off the hips using a catmull spline with two segments, sweeping it with a tapering radius, and deciding to skip adding a membrane between the tail or legs for now to keep things simple. Finally I'm making sure the hip root and eyes are set up properly before moving to apply countershading.

Double-checking that the countershade, mottle, and extrude helper signatures all match what I'm using, confirming the hips joint serves as the root with no parent, and verifying how the spine chain's joint array lines up so I can correctly grab the head joint. I'm also deciding to loop over left/right sides using a simple sign variable, and reasoning through the overall scale — this stylized bat ends up sized more like a large flying fox rather than a small fruit bat, but that's fine for this design. Time to write the final code.
